newsitem.title: USA: Higher hog, cattle prices lift U.S. farm price index.
newsitem.headline: Higher hog, cattle prices lift U.S. farm price index.

text.p: Higher prices for hogs, cattle and fruit lifted the farm price index by 0.9 percent in May, the U.S. Agriculture Department said Friday.
The index, a gauge of prices paid to farmers for their crops and livestock, rose to 107 from 106.1 in April. Compared to May 1996, the index was five points, or 4.5 percent lower.
Lower prices for lettuce, milk, corn and broiler chickens nearly outweighed the price increases.
Soybean prices rose 19 cents from April's level to average $8.42 per bushel. Wheat prices were down 2 cents, to average $4.09 per bushel. Corn was down 12 cents, to $2.68 a bushel.
Cattle prices were up 80 cents in May for an average $65.60 per 100 pounds, a hefty $10.90 higher than the gloomy times of one year ago.
Hog prices climbed to $58.00 per 100 pounds, up $4.20 from April and $1.20 better than last May.

"Fed cattle and beef cow prices were steady to down slightly because of large supplies of cattle on feed while shrinking supplies of lighter weight cattle led to higher feeder prices," the department said.
"Hog prices were supported by smaller than expected slaughter and prospects for export growth."
Broiler prices fell in May to 36.4 cents per pound, a drop of 0.7 cent. Turkey prices advanced by 1.7 cents per pound to average 41.2 cents per pound.
"Supplies of broilers and eggs continue to be large," the report said. "Cold storage holdings of turkeys decreased and placements are running 5 percent below a year ago."
Milk prices averaged $13.10 per 100 pounds for the month, down 30 cents from April.
Higher prices for strawberries, lemons, oranges and pears drove a 20 percent increase in the departments fruit and nuts index.
